extracted.intended_audience: aspiring screenwriters, novelists, and storytellers studying story structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the hierarchical units of dramatic design (beat → scene → sequence → act → story) and formal choices (Archplot/Miniplot/Antiplot) for constructing plotted narratives, with practical rules for turning value and shaping climax. Useful for writers structuring films, novels, or plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A BEAT is an exchange of behavior in action/reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beats are the smallest element of structure (not the dialogue pause). "Beat by Beat these changing behaviors shape the turning of a scene." Example: the "lovers break up" scene is built around six beats—distinct behaviors and changes of action/reaction (teasing → insults → threatening/daring → pleading/ridiculing → violence → decision/turning point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats must change behavior / turn action
rubrics_metrics.description: Beats should be distinct behaviors that change action/reaction and thereby shape scene turning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or writing, identify clear behavioral exchanges and changes; each beat should advance the scene's emotional or value charge toward a turning point. Avoid beats that are merely repetitive or fail to alter the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene (function and requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every true scene turns the value-charged condition of the character’s life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes cause relatively minor yet significant change; they should contain beats that build to a local turning point. A scene that doesn't change the character's value condition is failing as a scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence (definition and size)
rubrics_metrics.description: A SEQUENCE is a series of scenes—generally two to five—that culminates with greater impact than any previous scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequences aggregate scene changes into a larger movement; the capping scene of a sequence should deliver a more powerful, determinant change. It's useful to title each sequence to clarify its story purpose (e.g., 'getting the job' sequence takes character from NO JOB to JOB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title sequences to clarify purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Give each sequence a title that makes clear why it exists in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titling helps the writer keep the sequence's story purpose explicit (what value or condition it arcs), and ensures the sequence justifies its place rather than being filler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ACT is a series of sequences that peaks in a climactic scene which causes a major reversal of values, more powerful in its impact than any previous sequence or scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts collect sequences into a larger turning movement; act-climaxes should change the character’s life in major ways (inner life, relationships, fortunes). The degree of change distinguishes scene/sequence/act climaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story and Story Climax (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story is a series of acts that build to a last act climax or story climax which brings about absolute and irreversible change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final condition at story end must be an absolute, irreversible change in the value-charged situation of the protagonist. Earlier changes (scene/sequence/act) can be reversible, but the story climax should not be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use every line to turn or set up change
rubrics_metrics.description: Let every phrase of dialogue or line of description either turn behavior and action or set up the conditions for change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Micro-level discipline: avoid inert phrasing or descriptive detours that do not either cause a behavioral turning or prepare for one. This keeps narrative momentum and economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (definition and responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: To PLOT means to navigate through the dangerous terrain of story and when confronted by a dozen branching possibilities to choose the correct path. Plot is the writer’s choice of events and their design in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plotting entails deliberate choices about what to include, exclude, and the order of events; good plotting selects events that interconnect causally and thematically to deliver the desired arc and climax. Poor event choices or ordering collapse the inner journey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical Design / Archplot (core principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: CLASSICAL DESIGN means a story built around an active protagonist who struggles against primarily external forces of antagonism to pursue his or her desire, through continuous time, within a consistent and causally connected fictional reality, to a closed ending of absolute, irreversible change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archplot features (listed): Causality; Closed Ending; Linear Time; External Conflict; Single Protagonist; Consistent Reality; Active Protagonist. These are the default, time-tested choices for broadly satisfying dramatic stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miniplot (minimalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Miniplot reduces features of Classical Design—shrinking or compressing prominent aspects—while retaining enough classical elements that the film will still satisfy the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miniplot emphasizes simplicity and economy, often internalizing conflict and sometimes leaving somewhat open endings. It still requires careful execution; 'miniplot does not mean no plot.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiplot (antistructure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Antiplot reverses Classical Design: contradicting traditional forms to exploit or ridicule formal principles; it tends toward extravagance, inconsistent realities, and self-conscious overstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antiplot commonly uses fragmented time, coincidence over causality, inconsistent reality, and overtly symbolic or solipsistic perspectives. Intended to challenge or alienate mainstream audiences; requires its own internal consistency as an expression of the artist's subjective perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed Ending (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Story Climax of absolute, irreversible change that answers all questions raised by the telling and satisfies all audience emotion is a CLOSED ENDING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archplots commonly deliver closed endings; closure means the audience leaves with a rounded, satisfied emotional experience—nothing in doubt or unsated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open Ending (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Story Climax that leaves a question or two unanswered and some emotion unfulfilled is an OPEN ENDING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miniplot often uses open endings where most questions are answered but one or two trail for the audience to resolve. Open does not mean unfinished chaos—the remaining question(s) should be answerable and constrained by what came before.

rubrics_metrics.name: External vs Internal Conflict (focus choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archplot emphasizes external conflict (relationships, institutions, physical forces); Miniplot emphasizes internal conflict (inner thoughts, feelings, transformation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide where the dominant value struggle lies: in outer action (external) or inner psychological change (internal). This choice should drive scene and sequence design and how you dramatize change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single vs Multiple Protagonists (design implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical design usually places a single protagonist at the heart of the telling; splintering into multiple protagonists creates Multiplot, which minimizes the roller-coaster dynamic and spreads screen time among several stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Multiplot when you want a mosaic of short arcs; use single-protagonist Archplot to focus emotional investment and deep inner change in one character. Multiplot softens an Archplot’s intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active vs Passive Protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: An ACTIVE PROTAGONIST pursues desire by taking action against the world; a PASSIVE PROTAGONIST pursues desire inwardly and reacts to events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active protagonists suit Archplot (external drive); passive protagonists suit Miniplot (internalization). Passive leads can still produce deep change but need careful handling to avoid inertia on the screen/page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear vs Nonlinear Time (temporal design)
rubrics_metrics.description: LINEAR TIME arranges events in a temporal order the audience can follow; NONLINEAR TIME scrambles or fragments time so the audience cannot easily sort before/after.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linear ordering supports causal reading and classical emotional arc; nonlinear ordering can emphasize subjectivity, theme, or antistructure but risks audience confusion if used without clear purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality vs Coincidence (causal logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: CAUSALITY drives stories in which motivated actions cause effects that become causes of further effects; COINCIDENCE drives stories where unmotivated actions produce events that don't chain into further effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer causal chains for meaning and satisfying climax (Archplot). Coincidence can be used deliberately to express randomness, fragmentation, or absurdity (Antiplot), but overuse undermines narrative coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent vs Inconsistent Realities (world rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: CONSISTENT REALITIES are fictional settings with modes of interaction kept consistent throughout to create meaning; INCONSISTENT REALITIES mix modes so episodes jump from one reality to another to create absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you establish rules (even fantastical ones), maintain them unless you intentionally signal a different mode and accept the audience's disorientation. Inconsistent realities can be effective when expressing subjective perception, but risk alienating viewers if arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change vs Stasis / Nonplot
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories above the change/stasis line show life changing; Nonplot works remain in stasis and do not arc—the character’s value-charged condition at end is virtually identical to the opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your aim is 'story' proper, design arcs that change the protagonist meaningfully. Nonplot can still offer insight/portraiture but it is not a plotted story and should be treated as such, not mislabeled as plot-driven narrative.
